nameStory: American eelgrass gets its name from its long, ribbon-like leaves that sway gracefully underwater like swimming eels. It's also called 'tape grass' because those same narrow leaves look just like green tape streaming in the current. The name 'wild celery' comes from the fact that ducks and other waterfowl absolutely love to munch on it, just like we might snack on celery sticks!
description: American eelgrass is a completely underwater plant that looks like long green ribbons flowing in lakes, ponds, and slow rivers. Its narrow, tape-like leaves can grow up to 3 feet long, creating underwater meadows that provide important habitat for fish and food for waterfowl. Unlike many water plants that float on the surface, eelgrass stays completely submerged, rooted to the bottom with its leaves streaming upward toward the light. This native plant is a true aquatic species that never needs to come up for air!

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Long, narrow ribbon-like leaves that feel smooth and flexible, typically 1/4 to 3/4 inch wide and up to 3 feet long, growing directly from the base in clusters

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Completely submerged underwater plant that forms dense colonies or meadows, with leaves swaying gracefully in the current like underwater grass

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny, inconspicuous flowers that develop underwater on thin stalks, easily missed but sometimes visible as small bumps along the leaf bases

idTips.label: Roots
idTips.description: White, fibrous root system that anchors firmly into muddy or sandy lake and pond bottoms, often visible when plants are pulled up

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Leaves feel smooth and slippery when wet, somewhat like wet plastic tape, and are translucent enough that you can see veins running parallel down their length

habitat: American eelgrass thrives in the shallow waters of lakes, ponds, slow-moving rivers, and quiet coves throughout New England. It prefers areas with muddy or sandy bottoms where it can root securely, typically growing in water depths from 1 to 10 feet where sunlight can still penetrate. You'll often find it mixed with other aquatic plants like pondweeds and water lilies, creating diverse underwater plant communities.

seasonality.spring: New leaves begin emerging from winter rootstocks as water temperatures warm, appearing as fresh green ribbons reaching toward the surface.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season when the underwater meadows are at their fullest and most visible, with leaves streaming in long, graceful ribbons.
seasonality.fall: Leaves begin to yellow and break apart as the plant prepares for winter, with fragments often washing ashore after storms.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground parts die back completely, leaving only the root system alive in the mud to regrow next spring.

funFact: Canvasback ducks are so obsessed with eating American eelgrass that they'll migrate hundreds of miles just to find the best patches, and the plant makes up such a huge part of their diet that it actually affects the taste of the duck meat - hunters prize canvasbacks that have been feeding on wild celery beds!
confusionNotes: Don't confuse American eelgrass with marine eelgrass (Zostera marina) which grows in salt water along the coast - American eelgrass is strictly a freshwater plant. Also, it's easily distinguished from surface-floating plants like eel-grass pondweed because true American eelgrass stays completely underwater with its ribbon leaves streaming upward.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'eelgrass,' this plant is not related to marine eelgrass at all - they just happen to look similar with their long, ribbon-like leaves. The 'wild celery' name can also be confusing since it's not related to garden celery either, but waterfowl find it just as tasty and nutritious.
compareHints: Since American eelgrass is the only Vallisneria species in New England, compare it to other ribbon-leaved aquatic plants like eel-grass pondweed or water stargrass. The key difference is that eelgrass has much longer, more flexible leaves that grow in distinct clusters from the base, while pondweeds typically have leaves arranged along branching stems and water stargrass has much shorter, stiffer leaves.
